title: My Grandmother's Stories
paragraphs: Last weekend, Kamila visited her grandmother, Apai Raushan, in the old part of Uralsk. Apai Raushan is 78 years old and remembers life very differently from today. She lived in a small village near Oral when she was a child. There was no television, no internet, and no mobile phones. Life was simple but full of community spirit.

"We walked five kilometres to school every day," Apai Raushan told Kamila. "In winter, it was very cold, but we never missed a day. Our teacher was strict but fair. We all loved her." Kamila listened carefully and wrote down everything in her notebook. She wanted to remember every detail.

Apai Raushan also talked about food. "We cooked everything from scratch. Your great-grandmother baked bread every morning in a clay oven. We grew vegetables in our garden — onions, carrots, potatoes, and cucumbers. We never wasted anything." Kamila looked at the soft bread on the table and thought about how much work it used to take.

Life changed a lot in the 1960s and 1970s. Apai Raushan's family moved to Uralsk when she was eighteen. She studied at a teacher training college and graduated in 1966. "I taught primary school children for forty years," she said proudly. "I loved my job. Every child is a little miracle."

One story surprised Kamila the most. During a big storm in 1969, the river flooded the lower part of Uralsk. Apai Raushan helped her neighbours carry their furniture to higher ground. "We worked all night," she remembered. "Nobody complained. We just helped each other." Kamila felt deeply moved by this story of community and courage.

Before Kamila left, Apai Raushan gave her an old black-and-white photograph. In the photo, a group of young women stood in front of a school building, all smiling broadly. "That is me — third from the left," said Apai Raushan. Kamila studied the photo carefully. Her grandmother looked young, energetic, and full of dreams — just like Kamila herself today.
